query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing the nozzle-to-substrate distance to 300 mm on the HVAF-i7 torch increases particle velocity and deposition efficiency, yielding a significantly thicker FeCoNiCrAl bond coat compared to the baseline established at standard distances.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder with 15–45 μm particle size, previously deposited by HVAF-M3 with high-quality outcomes but now applied with the HVAF-i7 torch.
generation.intervention: Set the nozzle-to-substrate spray distance to a nozzle-specific value of 300 mm, ensuring that the spray plume and particle stream are optimized for increased velocity.
generation.conditions: Spraying performed under standard HVAF-i7 operating parameters in ambient conditions on substrates that include internal diameters as small as 120 mm and are intended for high-temperature application (up to ~900 °C).
generation.structural_mediator: A reduced stand-off distance enhances the in-flight kinetic energy of the particles, leading to improved splat formation and intersplat bonding while protocols for uniform coverage in restricted geometries are implemented.
generation.mechanism: A shorter spray distance decreases the travel time of the particles, reducing deceleration and in-flight oxidation. The increased impact velocity ensures better deformation and bonding, which builds up a thicker, denser coating.
generation.predicted_outcome: The as-sprayed coating will achieve a thickness increase of approximately 20–50% relative to the baseline produced at non-optimized distances, while maintaining low oxidation and consistent adhesion over both flat and complex (120 mm ID) surfaces.
generation.baseline: HVAF-i7 deposition using 15–45 μm feedstock at default spray distances, resulting in acceptable quality but inadequate thickness.
generation.boundary: This improvement holds so long as the increased particle velocity does not result in excessive local heating or oxidation; careful monitoring is required to maintain uniformity within small internal diameters.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvement depends on the precise balance between increased kinetic energy and potential minor oxidation effects; geometric constraints in small diameters could introduce variability.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct HVAF-i7 depositions on identical substrates (including internal features of 120 mm) with one set using a 300 mm spray distance and a control set at the default distance. Use identical 15–45 μm feedstock for both cases.
measurements: In-flight particle velocity (using diagnostic probes if available)
Oxide content and microstructure integrity (via SEM/EDX and XRD)
Adhesion strength (using standardized pull-off or scratch tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized 300 mm spray distance does not yield a statistically significant thickness increase (less than 10% improvement) or results in deteriorated adhesion/increased oxidation compared to the control, the hypothesis will be falsified.

papers.title: Oxidation Behavior of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 High-Entropy Alloy Powder.
papers.system: FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy used in HVOF-sprayed coatings
papers.approach: Variation of spray parameters (especially spray distance) to control in-flight oxidation and deposition efficiency
papers.findings: Increasing the spraying distance was found to decrease the coating thickness and increase porosity and oxidation due to lower particle kinetic energy and longer oxygen exposure.
papers.mechanism: Longer spray distance reduces particle kinetic energy, making them more susceptible to in-flight oxidation and scattering, which leads to thinner, more porous deposits.

papers.title: Comparative Study on the Thermal Performance of Cr-CrₓOy and YSZ-CoNiCrAlY Coatings Exposed at 900 °C.
papers.system: Conventional MCrAlY bond coats deposited by HVAF (or similar) deposition systems
papers.approach: Optimization of spray parameters with a focus on particle velocity and nozzle-specific spray distances (300–350 mm) to improve deposition efficiency
papers.findings: Studies reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency when using higher particle velocities and optimized spray distances, resulting in better bonding and potentially thicker deposits.
papers.mechanism: Increased particle velocity at shorter, nozzle-specific distances leads to improved momentum transfer and splat formation upon impact, enhancing overall deposition efficiency.

established: High-quality coatings with sufficient thickness have been achieved using HVAF-M3 with a 15–45 μm feedstock.
Spray deposition parameters such as spray distance and particle velocity crucially affect coating thickness, in-flight oxidation, and porosity.

approaches_tried.approach: Applying the same 15–45 μm feedstock on HVAF-i7 torch
approaches_tried.outcome: Yielded acceptable coating quality but insufficient coating thickness.

approaches_tried.approach: Optimizing spray distance (300–350 mm) along with higher particle velocity for MCrAlY bond coats
approaches_tried.outcome: Resulted in modest improvements in deposition efficiency.

mechanisms: Higher particle velocity increases kinetic energy, leading to more effective in-flight melting and splat formation; in turn, this improves deposition efficiency and coating thickness.
Longer spray distances reduce the kinetic energy of the particles, increasing their exposure to oxygen and causing in-flight oxidation and increased porosity.
disagreements: There is some uncertainty whether simply increasing particle velocity (by shortening spray distance) is sufficient or if adjustments in feedstock parameters (e.g., particle size distribution) might also be required to fully overcome the thickness limitation.
open_questions: Can the HVAF-i7 torch achieve coating thickness comparable to HVAF-M3 solely by optimizing spray distance and increasing particle velocity?

How will the optimized deposition parameters influence the as‐sprayed oxidation levels and long‐term durability of the bond coat during high-temperature service, especially in complex geometries (internal diameters as small as 120 mm)?
opportunities: Implement a single intervention by optimizing the spray distance to a nozzle-specific range (around 300–350 mm) to elevate the particle velocity for HVAF-i7 systems.
Combine this parameter tuning with careful monitoring of in-flight oxidation to secure a thicker, adherent bond coat while preserving coating integrity and high-temperature oxidation resistance.

Design controlled experiments that systematically vary spray distance to directly compare deposition thickness, oxidation levels, and adhesion performance relative to the 15–45 μm feedstock baseline under conditions relevant for internal diameters down to 120 mm.

directions.direction: Optimize the nozzle-to-substrate spray distance to achieve higher particle velocity
directions.assessment: Directly addresses deposition thickness by increasing particle kinetic energy. Evidence from studies on conventional MCrAlY bond coats supports a nozzle-specific spray distance (300–350 mm) as beneficial. This intervention respects the feedstock and chemistry constraints and is feasible with minor HVAF-i7 parameter adjustments.

directions.direction: Increase the propellant gas pressure to further accelerate particles
directions.assessment: By increasing the gas pressure, the particles’ velocity can be enhanced, potentially improving splat formation and deposit buildup. Although promising through kinetic energy control, care is needed to avoid excessive in-flight heating and oxidation. Evidence indirectly supports improved deposition with higher velocities.

directions.direction: Modify the nozzle geometry (e.g., use a more convergent design) to focus and accelerate the particle jet
directions.assessment: A nozzle with an improved convergent profile can deliver higher particle velocity and reduce particle scattering, addressing the thickness limitation. While the evidence primarily emphasizes spray distance and velocity, nozzle geometry is a plausible lever but may require more apparatus modification.

directions.direction: Introduce pre-heating of the substrate (or feedstock) to enhance splat formation and coating build‐up
directions.assessment: Pre-heating may improve bonding and allow the arriving particles to spread and fuse better, potentially increasing the coating thickness. However, caution is required as overheating might promote unwanted oxidation; the mechanism is supported by similar treatments in thermal spray technologies.

directions.direction: Slightly adjust the powder feed rate or powder concentration in the plume
directions.assessment: Changing the feed rate could increase deposition efficiency, though it is more of an indirect effect. Maintaining the optimal particle size while altering concentration may risk feedstock destabilization. This intervention is less directly connected to particle velocity improvements relative to the spray distance adjustment.
